item.source_title: Claude C. Hopkins, Scientific Advertising (1923; local copy a 2009 Snowball/BN Publishing reprint)
item.question: Chapter 9 rules out eccentricity; chapter 17 requires standing out. How does Hopkins hold both, and what selection rule does he give?
item.answer: He distinguishes two kinds of uniqueness: one that belittles and arouses resentment, and one that is refreshing, that enhances, and that we welcome and remember. Being eccentric or abnormal is not a distinction to covet; doing admirable things in a different way is. So the requirement is distinctiveness in manner and tone rather than in appearance or subject treatment. His selection rule is fit to audience: each advertiser is given an individuality best suited to the people he addresses — rugged and honest in a line where rugged honesty counts, a good fellow where choice is a matter of favour, an authority in other lines. He gives no way to classify a candidate persona in advance as refreshing rather than belittling, which is the decision the chapter exists to support, and he attaches no line, product or result to any of the three castings.

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 7 'The Case of the Disappearing Glass', sections 'Defining the Surface of Glassware' and 'Position the Light'
item.question: Compare a small bright highlight and a large dim one on the surface of a glass. What does the book say each does for the viewer, and what sets the difference in practice?
item.answer: They do opposite jobs. The tiny bright spots are distracting at the least and meaningless at best: they are too small and too bright to tell the viewer anything about surface detail or texture. A large highlight informs — it serves the constructive purpose of saying how the glass surface looks and feels. In practice the difference is set by how much of the relevant family of angles is filled with light, and, with a diffusion sheet, by the distance from the lamp head to the sheet: close in, only the centre of the sheet lights and the highlight is small and bright; pulled back, the whole sheet lights and reflects as a larger highlight. The authors add that the larger highlight should usually be kept dimmer, because a brightly lit whole sheet reflects as an obvious hard-edged rectangle that advertises a studio light and costs the scene its reality — and that strips of black tape on the sheet can make the reflection read as a window instead.
item.support: Ch. 7, 'Defining the Surface of Glassware', including the two matched highlight frames and the taped diffusion sheet.

source_terms: What are line extensions like light, clear, healthy, and fat-free actually telling you? That the regular products are not good for you.
Let sleeping brands lie.
item.claim: A specific failure mode with a specific diagnostic cue. Where a line extension is defined by the absence or reduction of something — light, clear, healthy, fat-free, aspirin-free — the authors say the extension communicates that the original product has the defect the extension removes. The manufacturer thereby argues against its own core brand. Their diagnostic test is to ask, before launch, what existing customers of the brand will conclude when they see the extension on the shelf.

mechanism.text: An extension carries an implicit comparison. Naming the new item by what it lacks asserts that the old item has it, and the assertion comes from the manufacturer, which is the one source the customer has no reason to disbelieve on that particular point. Bayer Select is their case: a company telling aspirin buyers that its own aspirin-free products are better.

item.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', sections 'Can your brand own something visual?' and 'Avoid style. Focus on substance.' (spine 15)
item.question: Sullivan endorses Krone's twenty-foot test and then makes a stronger claim of his own. State both, and identify the tension between this and his instruction to study a category's current visual conventions.
item.answer: Krone's requirement is a page style: you should be able to tell whose advertisement it is from a distance of twenty feet — and Sullivan notes what is interesting about it, which is that Krone was talking about print advertisements, not billboards. Sullivan's stronger claim is that the longer he is in the business the more convinced he is that art direction is where the major battle for brand building happens, because once a look is established and a design territory staked out, nobody else can use it without looking like your brand. He pairs it with an instruction to pull the look from the brand's own DNA rather than from current fashion, since riding every passing fad makes work trendy and derivative. The tension: knowing and avoiding a category's current clichés requires close attention to exactly the conventions this instruction says to ignore. He states both and does not reconcile them.
item.support: Krone is quoted from a 1968 trade interview; the stronger claim is Sullivan's own opinion, flagged by his phrasing, with no evidence. The colour-ownership examples are assertions about market perception with nothing measuring them. The tension is an extractor observation.
confounders: treating the twenty-foot test as calibrated; no viewing condition is specified
reading 'avoid style' as indifference to craft rather than as a warning against period fashion
assuming ownership of a colour or a look is established rather than asserted

source_terms: it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer
item.claim: Bijapurkar identifies a specific misdiagnosis and corrects it. When richer consumers began buying popular-segment rather than premium products, marketers called this "down-trading" and "many have suggested that this is the nature of the Indian consumer — mean and stingy." Her correction: "In fact, it is not the consumer who has 'down-traded' but the supplier who has 'up-traded' his offer and the popular and discount segments, in many cases, now offer a real value advantage in terms of equivalent if not better benefits at a lower price." She supplies the supply-side cause: unequal tax and duty incentives were withdrawn, forcing small manufacturers into open competition, which produced "rogue" marketers who refused to respect the unwritten price-performance rules, so consumers faced an explosion of new price-performance combinations. She gives the automotive instances — a 125cc motorcycle at a 100cc popular price, premium styling at discount prices, a B- segment car with premium features — and concludes that "the paradigm of premium-popular-discount = rich-middle income-poor is now quite irrelevant."

mechanism.text: Observed behaviour changed because the choice set changed, not because preferences did. When the price-performance frontier moves, a buyer whose preferences are unchanged will appear at a different point on the old segmentation — and an analyst who holds the segmentation fixed will attribute the movement to the buyer's character.

scope.conditions: Indian consumer markets after the withdrawal of differential tax and duty structures, principally FMCG, automotive, PCs and industrial water treatment, over roughly 1991-2009.

caveats.text: THE GENERAL SHAPE IS THE VALUABLE PART AND IT IS NOT INDIAN. Attributing a shift in observed behaviour to consumer character when the choice set moved is a reasoning error available anywhere. The specific instances are dated
the cases are named products and are checkable in principle, but no market-share, price or volume data is given for any of them

the author also offers a second, different explanation elsewhere for the same FMCG stagnation — a 'change confluence' in which consumer credit and durables purchases committed future income, forcing careful FMCG spending. The two explanations are compatible but are not reconciled, and the book presents each as sufficient in its own place

INSPECTED: Figure 4.2, the premium-popular-discount construct, was opened. It is a schematic price-against-performance diagram showing the traditional line and three 'new offering' positions below it; it carries no data and is an illustration of the argument, not evidence for it

source_stated_remedies: check whether the price-performance frontier moved before attributing a behaviour change to the buyer

item.source_title: Luke Sullivan, Hey Whipple, Squeeze This: The Classic Guide to Creating Great Advertising, 6th ed. (Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2022)
item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'A Controlled Daydream', section 'Get the visual clichés out of your system right away'; and Ch. 3 'Look at the competitors' advertising' (spines 15, 13)
item.question: Sullivan says visual clichés are not general but category-specific. What working procedure does that imply, and what stops this from being a blanket ban on familiar imagery?
item.answer: It implies research rather than taste: go and learn which images your category is currently using — visit the competitors' sites, watch their videos, study what they post — and then do not use those. His examples are category-bound: grandfathers flying kites with grandchildren in insurance, earnest bespectacled people with a screen reflected in their glasses in technology. The mechanism is availability, the same argument he makes about early ideas: a cliché is what the whole category already reaches for, so using it puts the brand inside the category's existing visual field rather than distinguishing it from it. What stops it being a blanket ban is his own endorsement of borrowed image equity: an established image given a spin and used in a new and unexpected way that relates to the product advantage is the metaphor he recommends. The prohibition is on unmodified reuse, not on familiar imagery.
item.support: Stated procedure and stated examples. Which images count as tired is judged by inspection and is time- and market-bound; his examples are American category conventions of his period.
confounders: treating the cliché list as universal rather than as something to be assembled per category
reading it as a prohibition on recognisable imagery, which his metaphor advice contradicts
assuming novelty alone resolves it — his metaphor condition requires the new use to relate to the product advantage

source_terms: avoid style, focus on substance
the soul of an idea instead of the width of its lapels
item.claim: Sullivan separates what changes from what does not and tells the maker to build on the second. Typefaces, design and art direction change; fads come and go. What people want — to look better, make more money, feel better, be healthy, and to have security, attention and achievement — he says is not likely to change. His instruction follows: direct the effort at those needs rather than at current visual affectations, and pull the look out of the brand's own DNA. He reports a consequence he says he noticed about simplicity specifically: it does not age, and the reduced advertisements in his simplicity chapter could be published tomorrow unchanged.

mechanism.text: Work anchored in a convention decays as the convention does; work anchored in a want that does not change has nothing to decay against. The observation about simplicity is the same argument in a stronger form — a piece with fewer elements has fewer places for a period style to attach.

item.question: What contrast does the source draw between Indian and contemporary Western posters, and what reason does it give for the Indian side of it?
item.answer: Western posters present a dramatic enigma — provocative images and text giving incomplete or paradoxical information — which the public must see the film to resolve, and they are supported substantially by text, including review quotations that function as 'the media seal of approval' plus studio, producer and director credits signalling the film's status. Indian posters 'rarely use text'. The reason given is distribution: with the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, 'text is seen as a cultural barrier' — text picks a language, and picking a language cuts the audience. From the 1980s it has been more common for only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director to appear, printed solely in English, because to the public those three figures are themselves a marker of the style, content and quality of the film.
item.support: 'text is seen as a cultural barrier'
item.confounders: The absence of text is not an aesthetic preference in this account; it is a response to a multilingual distribution constraint, and the three names that DO appear are doing the work the review quotations do elsewhere.

source_terms: text is seen as a cultural barrier

item.claim: Patel states a structural contrast between two poster traditions. Contemporary Western posters present a dramatic enigma — provocative images and text giving incomplete or paradoxical information — which requires the public to see the film to resolve it, and they are supported substantially by text, including review quotations that function as "the media seal of approval," plus studio, producer and director credits that signal the film's status. Indian posters, in contrast, "rarely use text": with the scale of national and international distribution the Indian industry enjoys, "text is seen as a cultural barrier." From the 1980s onward it has been more common for only the title and the names of the producer, director and music director to appear, printed solely in English, because to the public those three figures are a marker of the style, content and quality of the film. Indian posters accordingly "convey the familiarity of the form and content of the Indian film" rather than an enigma.

mechanism.text: Text has to be read in a language, so any text narrows the poster's reach across a multilingual distribution territory. Where the distribution is wide and the audience already knows the form, the poster's job shifts from posing a question to confirming a familiar promise, and that job can be done by images and by three names.

scope.conditions: Indian film posters from the 1980s onward against contemporary Western practice. Patel notes the earlier Indian convention was different — title and star names prominently in English with Hindi and Urdu titles in smaller lettering nearby — so this too is dated.

caveats.text: the comparison is drawn between two practices as the author characterises them; no sample of Western posters is enumerated and no count is given on either side

Patel notes the cost of the change she documents: more recent designs focusing on one narrative element are 'more universally understood' but 'convey less information about the culture in which they are produced'. That trade-off is stated by the source and is the most useful part of this object

source_stated_problems: text narrows a poster's reach across a multilingual distribution territory
source_stated_remedies: carry the message in recognisable images and in the three names that index style, content and quality

item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical, opening — the concrete-poems and cubistic-composition captions (spine 6)
item.question: Samara shows two ways of keeping difficult layouts readable. Describe both, and say what principle they share.
item.answer: In the first, a spread of concrete poems mitigates reading-sequence difficulty by positioning each poem's title so that it directs readers to the conventional location for text to start — upward and to the left; once the reader has entered from that familiar point, careful attention to the proximities of sequential words and phrases carries them through unexpected orientations, changes in spacing and other obstacles. In the second, a multi-plane cubistic composition integrates columns of relatively extensive text into its visual language while leaving the text situated primarily within open negative space, so it keeps its distinct identity and its legibility free of textural interference. The shared principle is that the difficulty is retained and localised rather than removed: one supplies a conventional entry point into an unconventional field, the other gives the text a protected zone inside a complex space. In neither case is the invention diluted; in both, one specific reading requirement is guaranteed.
item.support: Captions in "Considering the Practical in the Impractical": the concrete-poem titles directing readers to the conventional starting point and proximity carrying them onward; the cubistic composition keeping text within open negative space to preserve identity and legibility.
confounders: assuming the repair means simplifying the whole layout
treating the entry point as a decorative device rather than as the navigational concession it is
assuming the text must be separated from the composition entirely; in the second case it is integrated into the visual language and only protected from textural interference

item.definition_in_origin_frame: The differentiation advertising style contributes to a product that is not itself different from its competitors.
A product materially no different from its competitors, because manufacturers share technology and use the same research to set colour, size, design and taste.

source_terms: so many products are no different from their competitors

all you can hope to do is explain their virtues more persuasively than your competitors, and to differentiate them by the style of your advertising. This is the 'added value' which advertising contributes
item.claim: Many products are not different from their competitors, because manufacturers share technology and use the same research to set colour, size, design and taste. For such parity products the only available moves are to explain their virtues more persuasively and to differentiate by the style of the advertising. The source calls this the added value advertising contributes.

mechanism.text: Shared technology and shared research methods converge products on the same attributes, leaving no product-level difference to advertise.

scope.conditions: product categories where competing products are materially alike

caveats.text: the author adds that he is not sufficiently puritanical to hate himself for it, marking the practice as one he expects to be criticised

source_stated_problems: so many products are no different from their competitors
source_stated_remedies: explain the product's virtues more persuasively than competitors do
differentiate by the style of the advertising

intra_source_relations.note: rests on image being what consumers experience
the positively good approach is offered as the alternative to claiming superiority
